decks.title: Transport — Part 1: Importance, roadways and highway corridors
goals: Explain why an efficient transport network is essential for development
Explain the factors that affect road development in different terrains and list advantages and disadvantages of road transport
State the meaning and importance of expressways, National Highways, the NSEW Corridor and the Golden Quadrilateral

slides.heading: The arteries of a nation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — A tea packet from Assam, a car from Chennai and a sack of wheat from Punjab all reach your town by **transport**. India uses **land** transport (roads, railways, pipelines), **water** transport (inland, coastal, overseas) and **air** transport. In this part we study why transport matters and how India’s roads and highway corridors are organised.

rows: People and goods across the country

visual.alt: Table of the three modes of transport with types and uses

slides.narration: Namaste! Think of the tea from Assam, the cars from Chennai and the wheat from Punjab that reach your town. All of them travel by land, by water or by air. Transport links farms with markets, mines with factories and people with jobs. In this part we see why transport matters so much and how India’s roads and highway corridors are organised.

slides.heading: Why transport matters
slides.body_md: An efficient transport network is essential for **development**. It carries **raw materials** to factories and **finished goods** to markets; lets farmers sell **perishable** crops in distant cities; widens **trade**, both inside the country and abroad through ports; creates **jobs** in transport itself; supports **tourism**; helps **defence** and **disaster relief** reach border and remote areas quickly; and promotes **national integration** by bringing people of different regions together.

rows: Iron ore from Odisha to steel plants
Supplies to border and flood areas
People of all regions travel and meet

visual.alt: Table of five roles of transport with examples

slides.narration: A country cannot develop without good transport. It carries iron ore to steel plants and finished goods to shops. It lets an apple grower in Himachal sell fruit in Delhi before it spoils. It carries goods to ports for trade, gives jobs, brings tourists, helps soldiers and relief teams reach distant places, and brings people of different regions together.

slides.heading: Modes working together
slides.body_md: Modes **complement** one another. A consignment often moves by road from a farm or factory to a railway yard, by rail across the country, by road again to a port, and by ship overseas. **Pipelines** carry crude oil, gas and petroleum products. Each mode suits certain loads, distances and terrains — the skill is in combining them.

visual.alt: Flow of goods from a farm or factory by road, then rail, to a port and ship

slides.narration: Transport modes work best together. Goods often travel by truck from a farm or factory to a railway yard, by train across the country, by truck again to a port, and by ship to another country. Pipelines quietly carry oil and gas. Each mode suits certain loads and distances, and a good transport system joins them smoothly.

slides.body_md: Link transport to development.
slides.narration: Quick check. Transport links raw materials, factories and markets.

slides.heading: What affects road building?
slides.body_md: **Relief:** roads are easy and cheap to build on the **level plains**; in **mountains** they need hairpin bends, retaining walls, tunnels and bridges, and **landslides** block them. **Climate:** heavy rain and **floods** wash roads away (north-east India, coastal plains); **snow** closes high passes for months (Ladakh). **Rivers:** many bridges are needed on the plains and deltas. **Soil:** clayey soils turn to mud; sandy desert soils shift. **Population and economy:** dense, productive regions justify dense road networks. **Capital:** hill and border roads are very costly; the **Border Roads Organisation** builds and maintains strategic roads.

visual.alt: Table of factors that make road building easy or difficult

slides.narration: Roads are easy to build on flat plains but hard in the mountains, where engineers must cut hairpin bends, tunnels and walls, and landslides often block the way. Heavy rain and floods wash roads away, and snow closes high passes for months. Many rivers mean many bridges. And busy, crowded regions need and can pay for more roads than empty ones.

slides.heading: Worked example: a road to Tawang
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give three geographical reasons why building and keeping open a road to Tawang in the hills of Arunachal Pradesh is difficult, and suggest one solution.

**Step 1. Relief:** steep slopes need many bends, cuttings and bridges, raising cost.

**Step 2. Climate:** very heavy monsoon rain causes landslides; snow blocks high passes in winter.

**Step 3. Sparse population:** few users, so returns are low, though the road matters for defence.

**Solution:** the Border Roads Organisation builds all-weather roads and tunnels through the high passes.

visual.alt: Table of problems of a mountain road with causes and responses

slides.narration: Why is a road to Tawang so hard? The slopes are steep, so the road needs many bends, cuttings and bridges, which makes it costly. Heavy monsoon rain sets off landslides, and in winter snow can block the high passes. Few people live there, yet the road is vital for defence, so the Border Roads Organisation builds tunnels and all-weather roads.

slides.heading: Quick check: road building
slides.body_md: Identify a factor that makes road building difficult.
slides.narration: Quick check. Steep slopes, landslides, floods and snow make roads hard to build and keep open.

slides.heading: Roads: advantages and disadvantages
slides.body_md: **Advantages:** **door-to-door** service; flexible routes and timings; cheaper and quicker than rail for **short distances**; can climb steep, hilly terrain where railways cannot; ideal for **perishables** (milk, vegetables, fruit); act as **feeders** to railway stations, ports and airports; lower construction cost than railways. **Disadvantages:** costly and slow for **bulky goods over long distances**; **air pollution** and noise; **accidents** and congestion; damaged by heavy rain and floods; heavy fuel use.

rows: Costly for long hauls of bulky goods

visual.alt: Table of advantages and disadvantages of road transport

slides.narration: Road transport takes goods from door to door, runs at any time and on any route, and is cheapest for short trips. It climbs hills that trains cannot, and it is ideal for milk, fruit and vegetables. It also feeds stations, ports and airports. But for heavy goods over long distances it is costly and slow, and it causes pollution, noise, accidents and traffic jams.

slides.heading: Classes of roads and expressways
slides.body_md: **Expressways:** wide, multi-lane, **access-controlled** highways with no level crossings, built for fast, safe, long-distance traffic — the Mumbai–Pune Expressway (the first, opened in 2002), the Yamuna Expressway (Greater Noida to Agra) and the Agra–Lucknow Expressway. **National Highways:** main roads linking state capitals, big cities, ports and border areas; built and maintained by the **Central Government** (NHAI). **State Highways:** link state capitals with district towns (State Governments). **District roads** link district headquarters with towns; **village roads** link villages (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana). **Border roads** serve strategic areas.

visual.alt: Table of classes of roads with what they link and who builds them

slides.narration: Indian roads come in classes. Expressways are wide, fenced roads with no crossings, built for fast traffic, like the Mumbai Pune Expressway. National Highways join state capitals, big cities and ports and are looked after by the central government. State Highways, district roads and village roads carry traffic down to the smallest settlements, and border roads serve the frontier.

slides.heading: The Golden Quadrilateral and the NSEW Corridor
slides.body_md: The **Golden Quadrilateral (GQ)**, about 5,800 km of four- and six-lane highways, joins the four metropolitan cities **Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata**. The **North–South Corridor** links **Srinagar** with **Kanyakumari**, and the **East–West Corridor** links **Silchar** (Assam) with **Porbandar** (Gujarat); the two cross at **Jhansi**. Both were built under the National Highways Development Project. **Importance:** faster, safer movement of goods and people; lower fuel and vehicle costs; growth of industries and towns along the routes; national integration.

slides.narration: The Golden Quadrilateral is a ring of wide highways joining Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, the four great metropolitan cities. Across it run two long corridors: one from Srinagar in the north to Kanyakumari in the south, and one from Silchar in the east to Porbandar in the west. They meet at Jhansi. These roads cut travel times and help industry grow along them.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a truck journey
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A transporter must send machinery from a factory in Pune to a buyer in Kolkata. (a) Which highway system would the truck mainly use? (b) Give three benefits of these highways.

**(a)** It joins the Golden Quadrilateral near Mumbai or Pune and follows it via Chennai (or via Delhi) to Kolkata, using the Mumbai–Pune Expressway at the start.

**(b)** Four- and six-lane divided roads allow higher, steadier speeds; bypasses avoid town congestion, saving time and fuel; fewer accidents and less wear on vehicles lower costs.

visual.alt: Flow of a truck journey from Pune by expressway onto the Golden Quadrilateral to Kolkata

slides.narration: A truck from Pune would first use the expressway, then join the Golden Quadrilateral and follow it round to Kolkata. Because these highways are wide, divided and bypass crowded towns, the truck moves faster and more steadily, uses less fuel, suffers less wear and is less likely to crash. That lowers the cost of moving goods across the country.

slides.body_md: Recall the cities and corridors.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Transport is vital for industry, trade, farming, defence, relief and national integration; modes complement one another.
Road building depends on relief, climate, rivers, soil, population and capital.
Roads: door-to-door, flexible, good for short distances and hills; costly for bulky long hauls, polluting.
Expressways (access-controlled), National Highways (Central Government), State, district, village and border roads.
Golden Quadrilateral: Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata; NSEW: Srinagar–Kanyakumari and Silchar–Porbandar, crossing at Jhansi.

visual.alt: Summary table of highway networks and key cities

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Transport carries the goods and people that development depends on, and the modes work best together. Road building is shaped by relief, climate, rivers and population. Roads are flexible and reach everywhere but are costly over long distances. The Golden Quadrilateral links the four metropolitan cities, and two corridors cross the country, meeting at Jhansi.

decks.title: Transport — Part 2: Railways, airways and waterways
goals: Explain why the rail network is dense in the northern plains and sparse in hilly and desert areas
Explain why air transport is important for remote and hilly areas despite its high cost
Compare inland and coastal waterways and state their advantages and limitations
Compare modes using freight cost and time

slides.heading: Rails, wings and water
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **Indian Railways** is one of the largest railway systems in the world under a single management. **Airways** shrink great distances, and **waterways** — rivers, canals, backwaters and the coast — carry heavy loads cheaply. Each mode has its own geography.

visual.alt: Table of railways, airways and waterways with best use and main limitation

slides.narration: In this part we look at railways, airways and waterways. India’s railways form one of the biggest networks in the world under one management. Aircraft cross mountains and seas in hours. Rivers, canals and the coast carry heavy cargo cheaply. Each mode suits some places and some goods better than others, and geography explains why.

slides.heading: Where railways are dense, and why
slides.body_md: The rail network is **densest in the northern plains** (Punjab to West Bengal): flat land, fertile soil, **dense population**, many towns, farms and industries generating traffic, and low building costs. It is **sparse** in the **Himalayas and the north-east hills** (steep slopes, landslides, heavy rain, need for tunnels and bridges), in the **Thar desert** (shifting sand dunes, sparse population, little water) and in **thick forests** and **swampy deltas**. The **Konkan Railway** (1998) along the Western Ghats coast needed many tunnels and bridges, showing the cost of difficult terrain.

visual.alt: Table of regions with dense or sparse rail networks and reasons

slides.narration: Railways are thickest on the northern plains, where the land is flat, people are many and farms and factories create plenty of traffic. They are thin in the Himalayas and the north-east, where steep slopes, landslides and heavy rain make building hard, and in the Thar desert, where sand shifts and few people live. The Konkan Railway needed hundreds of tunnels and bridges.

slides.heading: Railway gauges
slides.body_md: The **gauge** is the distance between the two rails. **Broad gauge** (1.676 m) carries the heaviest, fastest traffic and is now the main gauge; **metre gauge** (1 m) and **narrow gauge** (0.762 m or 0.610 m) survive mainly on hill and branch lines such as Kalka–Shimla. Under **Project Unigauge**, most lines have been converted to broad gauge so that trains need not stop and transfer goods where gauges change.

slides.narration: The gauge is the distance between the rails. Broad gauge is the widest and carries most of India’s trains. Metre gauge and narrow gauge are found mainly on hill and branch lines, such as the little line from Kalka to Shimla. Most lines have been converted to broad gauge, so goods no longer need to be shifted from one train to another where the gauge changed.

slides.heading: Quick check: railways
slides.body_md: Explain the density of the rail network.
slides.narration: Quick check. The rail network is densest on the flat, crowded, productive northern plains.

slides.heading: Worked example: comparing rail density
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** State P (plain, illustrative) has 2500 km of railway in 50000 sq km; State Q (hilly, illustrative) has 400 km in 80000 sq km. (a) Find the rail density of each, in km per 1000 sq km. (b) Explain the difference.

**(a)** P $= \dfrac{2500}{50000} \times 1000 = 50$; Q $= \dfrac{400}{80000} \times 1000 = 5$.

**(b)** P is flat, densely populated and productive, so lines are cheap to build and well used; Q’s steep slopes, landslides and sparse population make railways costly and little used.

visual.alt: Table of illustrative rail length, area and density for two states

slides.narration: Divide the length of track by the area and multiply by one thousand to get kilometres of railway for every thousand square kilometres. The plain state has fifty, the hilly state only five, ten times fewer. The plain state is flat, crowded and busy, so railways are cheap and well used, while the hilly state’s slopes, landslides and scattered villages make them costly.

slides.heading: Railways: advantages and disadvantages
slides.body_md: **Advantages:** cheapest land transport for **bulky goods** (coal, iron ore, food grains, cement) over **long distances**; carry huge numbers of passengers cheaply; safer and less affected by weather than roads; use less fuel and pollute less per tonne-km than trucks; promote national integration and employ many people. **Disadvantages:** **fixed routes and timetables**, no door-to-door service; very **high capital cost**; difficult and costly in **hilly** and desert terrain; goods must be loaded and unloaded at stations (transshipment); less economical for short distances.

visual.alt: Table of advantages and disadvantages of railways

slides.narration: Railways move coal, ore, grain and cement cheaply over long distances, and carry millions of passengers at low fares. They are safer than roads, less troubled by weather, and use less fuel for each tonne carried. But they run only on fixed tracks and timetables, cost a great deal to build, struggle in hills and deserts, and need trucks at each end.

slides.heading: Airways
slides.body_md: **Advantages:** the **fastest** mode; crosses **mountains, deserts, forests and seas** with no need for roads or tracks; vital for **remote and hilly areas** — the **north-east**, **Ladakh**, the **Andaman and Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** islands — where land routes are long or blocked; essential in **floods, earthquakes** and other **emergencies**; important for **defence**, tourism and business travel; carries **perishable and high-value** goods (flowers, medicines, electronics). **Disadvantages:** **very high cost** of fuel, aircraft and airports; small capacity for bulky goods; disrupted by **fog**, storms and poor visibility; noise and emissions.

visual.alt: Table of advantages and disadvantages of air transport

slides.narration: Air transport is the fastest of all and does not care about mountains, forests or seas. That makes it vital for the hilly north-east, Ladakh and the island groups, where roads are long or blocked, and for rushing help to flood and earthquake areas. It carries flowers, medicines and electronics quickly. But it is very costly, carries little bulky cargo and is grounded by thick fog.

slides.heading: Quick check: airways
slides.body_md: Explain the value of air transport in remote areas.
slides.narration: Quick check. Aircraft cross mountains and seas, so they serve remote hills and islands despite the cost.

slides.heading: Inland and coastal waterways
slides.body_md: **Inland waterways** use rivers, canals, lakes and backwaters. National Waterways include **NW-1** on the **Ganga–Bhagirathi–Hooghly** (Prayagraj to Haldia), **NW-2** on the **Brahmaputra** (Sadiya to Dhubri) and **NW-3**, the **West Coast Canal** of Kerala (Kollam to Kottapuram); many more were declared in 2016. Barges on the Mandovi and Zuari in Goa long carried iron ore to the coast. **Limitations:** water levels fall in the dry season; **silting** and shifting channels; rapids and falls in peninsular rivers; slow. **Coastal shipping** moves cargo between Indian ports — for example coal from Paradip to power stations in Tamil Nadu — cheaply, but it needs good ports and is affected by monsoon storms.

rows: NW-1 Ganga, NW-2 Brahmaputra, NW-3 Kerala
Coal from Paradip to Tamil Nadu
Cheap for bulky cargo, eases rail load

visual.alt: Table comparing inland waterways and coastal shipping

slides.narration: Inland waterways use rivers, canals and backwaters, such as the Ganga between Prayagraj and Haldia, the Brahmaputra in Assam and the West Coast Canal of Kerala. They are cheap but slow, and in the dry season the water may be too shallow; silt and shifting channels are further problems. Coastal ships carry heavy cargo such as coal from port to port, easing the load on railways.

slides.heading: A seaport
slides.body_md: Ports link sea routes with the land. A **breakwater** shelters the harbour from waves; a **dredged channel** gives ships enough depth; **berths, cranes and warehouses** handle cargo; **rail and road links** connect the port with its **hinterland** (the area it serves). Natural harbours (Mumbai, Visakhapatnam, Kochi) need less building; river ports such as Kolkata need constant dredging, which is why **Haldia** was developed downstream.

slides.narration: This chart compares the cost of carrying one tonne for one kilometre. Waterways are the cheapest, then rail, then road, while air is many times dearer. The cheapest modes are also the slowest. So heavy, low value goods such as coal and ore go by water or rail, while fresh flowers, medicines and urgent parcels pay for road or air.

slides.heading: Worked example: choosing a mode
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 200 tonnes of cement must travel 800 km. Using the illustrative costs and speeds, find (a) the cost by road and by rail, (b) the saving by rail as a percentage of the road cost, and (c) the time by road and by rail.

**(a)** Road $= 2.5 \times 200 \times 800 = 400000$ rupees; rail $= 1.5 \times 200 \times 800 = 240000$ rupees.

**(b)** Saving $= \dfrac{400000 - 240000}{400000} \times 100 = 40$%.

**(c)** Road $= 800 \div 40 = 20$ h; rail $= 800 \div 25 = 32$ h. Rail is cheaper but slower — fine for cement, which does not spoil.

visual.alt: Table of illustrative cost and time for moving cement by road and by rail

slides.narration: Multiply the cost per tonne kilometre by the tonnes and the kilometres. By road the cement costs four lakh rupees to move, by rail only two lakh forty thousand, a saving of forty per cent. Divide distance by speed for the time: twenty hours by road and thirty two by rail. Cement does not spoil, so the cheaper, slower railway is the sensible choice.

notes.title: Transport — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Importance and modes of transport
sections.body_md:
- **Importance:** raw materials to industry; goods to markets; perishables reach distant cities; internal and foreign trade; jobs; tourism; defence and disaster relief; national integration.
- **Modes:** land (roads, railways, pipelines), water (inland, coastal, overseas), air.
- Modes **complement** one another: road → rail → port → ship is a common chain.

key_terms.definition_md: The area served by a port or transport centre, from which goods come and to which goods go.

visual.alt: Table of modes of transport and their types

sections.heading: 2. Roadways
sections.body_md:
- **Factors:** relief (plains easy; mountains need bends, tunnels, bridges; landslides); climate (heavy rain and floods; snow on high passes); rivers (bridges); soil (mud, shifting sand); population and economic activity; capital.
- **Advantages:** door-to-door; flexible; cheap and quick for short distances; reach hills and villages; good for perishables; feeders to rail, ports and airports; cheaper to build than railways.
- **Disadvantages:** costly for bulky goods over long distances; pollution and noise; accidents and congestion; damaged by rain and floods.
- **Border Roads Organisation** builds strategic roads in border and hill areas.

key_terms.definition_md: A road that brings traffic to a railway station, port or airport.

visual.alt: Table of two advantages and two disadvantages of roads

sections.heading: 3. Highways and corridors
sections.body_md:
| Road | Meaning or route | Built by |
|---|---|---|
| Expressway | Multi-lane, access-controlled, no level crossings (Mumbai–Pune, Yamuna, Agra–Lucknow) | Central or State agencies |
| National Highway | Links state capitals, big cities, ports, borders | Central Government (NHAI) |
| Golden Quadrilateral | About 5,800 km joining Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata | NHDP |
| North–South Corridor | Srinagar to Kanyakumari | NHDP |
| East–West Corridor | Silchar to Porbandar | NHDP |

The two corridors cross at **Jhansi**. Importance: faster, safer, cheaper movement; growth of industry and towns along routes; national integration.

key_terms.definition_md: A wide, multi-lane, access-controlled highway with no level crossings, built for fast traffic.
The highway network joining Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.

visual.alt: Table of the two corridors and their ends

sections.heading: 4. Railways
sections.body_md:
- **Dense** in the northern plains: flat land, dense population, farms and industries, low building cost.
- **Sparse** in the Himalayas and the north-east (steep slopes, landslides, heavy rain), the Thar (shifting sand, few people), forests and deltas.
- **Gauges:** broad 1.676 m, metre 1 m, narrow 0.762 m or 0.610 m; **Project Unigauge** converts lines to broad gauge.
- **Advantages:** cheap for bulky goods over long distances; huge capacity; safer; less fuel per tonne-km; national integration.
- **Disadvantages:** fixed routes and timetables; high capital cost; hard in hills and deserts; transshipment.
- **Konkan Railway** (1998): many tunnels and bridges along the Western Ghats coast.

key_terms.definition_md: The distance between the two rails of a railway track.

sections.heading: 5. Airways
sections.body_md:
- **Advantages:** fastest; crosses mountains, deserts, forests and seas; vital for the north-east, Ladakh, Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep; emergencies and defence; perishable and high-value goods; tourism.
- **Disadvantages:** very costly; small capacity for bulky goods; affected by fog and storms; noise and emissions; needs airports.

key_terms.definition_md: Links by air between places, especially important where land routes are long or blocked.

visual.alt: Table of remote areas and why air transport matters there

sections.heading: 6. Waterways and comparing modes
sections.body_md:
- **Inland:** NW-1 Ganga–Bhagirathi–Hooghly (Prayagraj–Haldia); NW-2 Brahmaputra (Sadiya–Dhubri); NW-3 West Coast Canal (Kollam–Kottapuram). Limitations: low water in the dry season, silting, shifting channels, rapids in peninsular rivers, slow.
- **Coastal:** cargo between Indian ports (coal from Paradip to Tamil Nadu); cheap for bulky goods; needs ports; monsoon storms.
- **Advantages of waterways:** cheapest for heavy, bulky goods; low fuel use and pollution; natural routes.
- **Freight cost** = rate per tonne-km × tonnes × km. **Time** = distance ÷ speed. **Rail density** = track length ÷ area × 1000.

One tonne of goods carried one kilometre; used to compare freight costs.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Listing Bengaluru instead of Chennai in the Golden Quadrilateral.
- Placing NW-2 on the Ganga (it is on the Brahmaputra).
- Saying roads are cheapest for bulky goods over long distances.
- Calling air transport unimportant because it is costly, without mentioning remote areas.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Reasons (1 mark each): one clear geographical cause with a named region.
- Advantages or disadvantages (1 mark each): distinct points, not repeats.
- Corridors (2 marks): four cities; or two corridors with their ends.
- Data (2–3 marks): working shown, answer with unit.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Give two reasons why transport is called the lifeline of a country’s economy. [2]

(b) With an example, show how different modes of transport complement one another. [2]

(c) Suggest the most suitable mode for each of these and give a reason: (i) iron ore from Bailadila to Visakhapatnam port, (ii) fresh fish from Kochi to Delhi in a day, (iii) vegetables from villages near Nashik to the town market. [3]

(d) Some planners want more freight moved by rail and water instead of by road. Give three reasons in support of this view. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) It carries raw materials to industries and goods to markets, so production and trade can grow; it links regions and people, supporting jobs, relief, defence and national integration.

(b) For example, rice from Karnal goes by truck to a container depot, by train to Mundra port and by ship abroad; road gives local collection, rail the cheap long haul and the ship the overseas link.

(c) (i) Rail — bulky ore over a long distance is moved cheaply. (ii) Air — the fish is perishable and must arrive quickly. (iii) Road — short, door-to-door trips to the market.

(d) Rail and water cost less per tonne-km for bulky goods; they use less fuel and cause less pollution per tonne carried; shifting heavy loads off highways reduces congestion, accidents and road damage.

questions.stem_md:
Study these illustrative freight rates and speeds: Road ₹2.5 per tonne-km at 40 km/h; Rail ₹1.5 per tonne-km at 25 km/h; Inland waterway ₹1.0 per tonne-km at 10 km/h; Air ₹15.0 per tonne-km at 500 km/h.

(a) Calculate the cost of moving 400 tonnes of goods 900 km by rail and by road. [2]

(b) By what percentage is the rail cost lower than the road cost? [2]

(c) Calculate the time taken for the 900 km journey by road, by rail and by inland waterway. [3]

(d) Recommend a mode, with a reason, for (i) cement for a building site 900 km away, (ii) mangoes for a market 900 km away and (iii) urgently needed machine parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Rail $= 1.5 \times 400 \times 900 = 540000$ rupees; road $= 2.5 \times 400 \times 900 = 900000$ rupees.

(b) $\dfrac{900000 - 540000}{900000} \times 100 = 40$%.

(c) Road $= 900 \div 40 = 22.5$ h; rail $= 900 \div 25 = 36$ h; waterway $= 900 \div 10 = 90$ h.

(d) (i) Rail — bulky, non-perishable goods are cheapest by rail. (ii) Road — mangoes are perishable, and a truck is faster than a goods train and delivers to the market door. (iii) Air — the parts are small, valuable and urgent, so speed justifies the cost.
